# Open Score: Orientation, Speed and Trajectory Measured Before Release, Not Separation

**What it is** — ESPN's receiver tracking metrics (RTM) have three parts: open score, catch score and yards-after-catch (YAC) score (teg9SfzpMy0 [04:06]). Panelists (the host introduces Seth Walder, Brian Burke and Allison Labs, caption spelling; the auto-captions do not label who speaks) describe open score as how open a receiver gets, and say it is not just the distance to the closest defender (teg9SfzpMy0 [06:12], [06:45]). The model uses x-y tracking positions plus more:
- **Orientation:** in a slant on fourth and four, the defender is within about a yard and a half at ball arrival, but the receiver faces where the ball is going and the defender is out of position, so the model scores him open (teg9SfzpMy0 [05:41], [06:12]).
- **Speed and trajectory:** on a play where the receiver looks open in a still frame, he is going 9 mph and the defender 13 mph, and the defender is coming faster and undercuts the route; the model scores him not open and the pass is broken up (teg9SfzpMy0 [09:21], [09:51]). On a hitch, the receiver is going 4.6 mph and the defender 10.3, and the model anticipates separation (teg9SfzpMy0 [07:47], [08:19]).
- **Untargeted receivers get credit:** the question asked of the receiver is only whether he got open (teg9SfzpMy0 [07:16], [07:47]).
- **Timing:** the model looks at 0.2 seconds before pass release, because in zone coverage defenders collapse on the target and leave untargeted receivers open (teg9SfzpMy0 [08:19], [08:50]).
- **Gravity:** extra credit when a receiver draws multiple defenders within a threshold (teg9SfzpMy0 [47:18], [47:49]).

**Why it works** — The panelists' reasoning is that open is "a different thing" from separation and a model that only used the straight-line distance would mislabel both cases above (teg9SfzpMy0 [06:12], [06:45]). The captions give no model internals for open score. A panelist says catch score uses a position-invariant convolutional neural network to estimate catch probability (teg9SfzpMy0 [23:47], [24:17]); whether open score uses the same network is not said. Inference: a measure built from positions, directions and speeds can separate a receiver who looks open from one who is open.

**When to apply** — When a single distance or "separation" number is being used as the measure of an athlete's success. Eric's baseline: force plate reporting follows an output, driver and strategy framework (adopted practice, the framework is Hawkin Dynamics' own), with extra metrics added "only with a specific, defensible rationale." Inference: the lesson here is similar, not identical: a single output value (distance) hides the drivers (orientation, speed, trajectory).

**When NOT to apply** — Illustrated with a handful of clips, mostly one receiver (AJ Brown), and no numbers on accuracy in the captions. `untested`. The data are NFL tracking data with x and y only, no z-axis (teg9SfzpMy0 [46:15]), no game-leverage context (teg9SfzpMy0 [46:46], [47:18]) and no quarterback progression (teg9SfzpMy0 [45:15]). A panelist says the right timing might be a fraction of a second before or after 0.2 seconds, and that is unknown without the progression data (teg9SfzpMy0 [45:45]). The stated purpose is fan content, not team use (teg9SfzpMy0 [02:03]).

**Example** — The panel's: AJ Brown scores highest in the league midseason, an overall 86, five points above the next player (the captions give "Travis Kelsey," a caption spelling) (teg9SfzpMy0 [03:05]).

# Open Score: Orientation, Speed and Trajectory Measured Before Release, Not Separation

**What it is** — ESPN's receiver tracking metrics (RTM) have three parts: open score, catch score and yards-after-catch (YAC) score (teg9SfzpMy0 [04:06]). Panelists (the host introduces Seth Walder, Brian Burke and Allison Labs, caption spelling; the auto-captions do not label who speaks) describe open score as how open a receiver gets, and say it is not just the distance to the closest defender (teg9SfzpMy0 [06:12], [06:45]). The model uses x-y tracking positions plus more:
- **Orientation:** in a slant on fourth and four, the defender is within about a yard and a half at ball arrival, but the receiver faces where the ball is going and the defender is out of position, so the model scores him open (teg9SfzpMy0 [05:41], [06:12]).
- **Speed and trajectory:** on a play where the receiver looks open in a still frame, he is going 9 mph and the defender 13 mph, and the defender is coming faster and undercuts the route; the model scores him not open and the pass is broken up (teg9SfzpMy0 [09:21], [09:51]). On a hitch, the receiver is going 4.6 mph and the defender 10.3, and the model anticipates separation (teg9SfzpMy0 [07:47], [08:19]).
- **Untargeted receivers get credit:** the question asked of the receiver is only whether he got open (teg9SfzpMy0 [07:16], [07:47]).
- **Timing:** the model looks at 0.2 seconds before pass release, because in zone coverage defenders collapse on the target and leave untargeted receivers open (teg9SfzpMy0 [08:19], [08:50]).
- **Gravity:** extra credit when a receiver draws multiple defenders within a threshold (teg9SfzpMy0 [47:18], [47:49]).

**Why it works** — The panelists' reasoning is that open is "a different thing" from separation and a model that only used the straight-line distance would mislabel both cases above (teg9SfzpMy0 [06:12], [06:45]). The captions give no model internals for open score. A panelist says catch score uses a position-invariant convolutional neural network to estimate catch probability (teg9SfzpMy0 [23:47], [24:17]); whether open score uses the same network is not said. Inference: a measure built from positions, directions and speeds can separate a receiver who looks open from one who is open.

**When to apply** — When a single distance or "separation" number is being used as the measure of an athlete's success. Eric's baseline: force plate reporting follows an output, driver and strategy framework (adopted practice, the framework is Hawkin Dynamics' own), with extra metrics added "only with a specific, defensible rationale." Inference: the lesson here is similar, not identical: a single output value (distance) hides the drivers (orientation, speed, trajectory).

**When NOT to apply** — Illustrated with a handful of clips, mostly one receiver (AJ Brown), and no numbers on accuracy in the captions. `untested`. The data are NFL tracking data with x and y only, no z-axis (teg9SfzpMy0 [46:15]), no game-leverage context (teg9SfzpMy0 [46:46], [47:18]) and no quarterback progression (teg9SfzpMy0 [45:15]). A panelist says the right timing might be a fraction of a second before or after 0.2 seconds, and that is unknown without the progression data (teg9SfzpMy0 [45:45]). The stated purpose is fan content, not team use (teg9SfzpMy0 [02:03]).

# Cluster Players on Physical and Psychological Scores Together to Find Types, Not Single Scores

**What it is** — The second speaker (caption spelling "Charles sheram") argues that the psychological characteristics had been studied "really in isolation", so the next step is the multivariate profile: "different types of players who have different constellations" and how each relates to "derailment or risk factors" (40NV3_u9tYY [19:44], [20:14]). Method: cluster analysis and mixture models, borrowed from market research (profiling customers by behavior and attitude), applied to 2014 to 2016 data (40NV3_u9tYY [21:16], [21:46], [22:16]). Inputs: coach-rated physical talent plus the psychological scores, shown as z-scores (40NV3_u9tYY [22:16], [22:47]). Output: nine profiles, for example:
- Cluster 7: above average on physical and on the psychological scores, "the whole package" (40NV3_u9tYY [22:47]).
- Cluster 9: above average psychologically, less physically talented (40NV3_u9tYY [22:47]).
- Cluster 3: physically talented, weak on teammate, leadership, preparedness and dependability (40NV3_u9tYY [23:18]).
- Cluster 6: low on everything (40NV3_u9tYY [24:19]).
The speaker proposes tagging risk factors and success factors to each cluster and, as a risk-management idea, avoiding or "pricing in" the risk like insurance (40NV3_u9tYY [20:14], [23:18]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism beyond the claim that "there's a lot of ways to be a successful football player" (40NV3_u9tYY [25:20]). Inference: clustering preserves combinations (strong body and weak habits, or the reverse) that a single composite score averages away.

**When to apply** — As a design for profiling athletes on more than one axis. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q3): "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q3) Inference: a Baylor version would start from a decision (a recruiting, roster or development question) and then ask whether any two-axis profile informs it. The talk shows no cluster results for college athletes.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the talk shows a model result with no validation of the clusters shown, no cluster sizes, no position breakdowns and no confidence intervals. The "physical" axis is the coaches' rating, not a measurement. The cluster count (nine) is the result of the speaker's analysis; the speaker does not say how it was chosen. Inference (40NV3_u9tYY [00:03], a co-author is "at the NFL combine assessing the players"): the speakers run the assessment (see the criterion-validation entry). The method is described for NFL players, rookie to early career; it should not be applied to Baylor athletes without Baylor's own data and a defined outcome.

**Example** — The speaker's own comparison: cluster 3 (strong physically, weak psychologically) against cluster 9 (the reverse), described as "almost the mere opposites" (caption spelling; Inference: "mirror opposites") with the same failure rate (40NV3_u9tYY [25:20]; see the bust-rate entry).

# Validating a Causal Metric When the True Effect Cannot Be Observed

**What it is** — Ben Jenkins notes that with observational data "we don't have the underlying causal effect" (JHgeEo3n1do [08:10], [08:40]), so he checks the metric indirectly (JHgeEo3n1do [07:09] to [09:10]):
1. **Face validity against honors:** top-10 rankings by position (defensive end, defensive tackle, outside and inside linebacker), with All-Pro and Pro Bowl players marked; he reports a "much better correlation" than supervised models (JHgeEo3n1do [07:09], [07:39]).
2. **Team-level aggregation:** mean individual EPS plotted against mean individual EPA for tacklers shows a strong negative correlation, which he says helps explain 41% of the variance in tackle play outcomes (JHgeEo3n1do [07:39], [08:10]).
3. **Synthetic data:** against independent models, his model has "significantly higher R-squared" and "much lower RMSE"; no values are given (JHgeEo3n1do [08:40]).
4. **Salary rank:** better ranking of non-rookie players by salary and by Pro Bowl status (JHgeEo3n1do [08:40]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's argument is that individual causal estimates that aggregate to team results and match honors are capturing "some of the genuine defensive value, not just the statistical artifacts" (JHgeEo3n1do [08:10]). The talk does not say why salary and honors should be unbiased proxies. Inference: honors and salaries are themselves partly produced by tackle counts, the quantity he criticizes, so agreement with them is weak evidence.

**When to apply** — As a checklist when someone presents a model with no ground truth: ask what the synthetic-data test knew that the model did not, what outside labels were used, and whether those labels share the model's bias. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q2a) uses "standard deviations and SWC to diagnose signal versus noise" for individualized thresholds (Explicit). Inference: that is a within-athlete noise check; the checks above are between-player, a different question.

R-squared, RMSE, rank correlations and salary comparisons are stated as better with no values (JHgeEo3n1do [08:40]). `untested`. Validation is by synthetic data and honors, not by a known true effect, and the speaker's claims of being first and of better ranking are his own in a competition presentation. Not a recipe for non-NFL data.

# Keep the Load Record of the Session in Which an Injury Occurs

**What it is** — The speaker (Luke Bourne, caption spelling; named because the introduction lists "Luke Bourne and Patrick Ward" as presenters, Patrick hands over with "turn it over to Luke" at [10:10], and this passage refers back to "what Patrick was saying before" at [16:47]) says earlier studies did not use same-session load for a simple reason: when a player is injured mid-session, that session's data is "censored" or thrown out. His example is that nobody is going to "carefully extract the GPS unit" in the middle of the field during an NFL practice (TIRINmtZOu0 [17:18], [17:49]). The result is that the analysis sees load before the injury session but not the intensity of the session itself, which is the variable the speakers argue matters most (see [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]]). The speaker says analyses "need to account for" the session load in that session (TIRINmtZOu0 [17:49]) and names survival models (how intense it was until the moment of injury) as one route (TIRINmtZOu0 [18:19]). Inference: the heuristic is to make sure the injured session's load, or at minimum its planned intensity, is saved.

Contested: the sibling entry [[framework--injury-coding-and-censoring-rules-for-load-analysis]] (TbYgc6_qQzo, Patrick Ward, [04:36], [12:15] to [12:47]) removes the injured-and-removed session from the data for that injury day, so the shortened session does not pull loads down, while this talk names that same removal ("censored, thrown out") as the reason earlier analyses missed same-session load. The two talks share people (Patrick Ward presents TbYgc6_qQzo alone and thanks "Luke Bourne" as a co-author at TbYgc6_qQzo [17:54]; both present TIRINmtZOu0), and the two positions are not reconciled in the captions. Treat the choice as open and state which rule a study used.

**Why it works** — The speaker's account is about missing data, not physiology: without the session's own load, a model cannot separate it from the prior-load ratio. The speaker gives no figure for how much data is lost. Inference: an injured athlete's device often stops mid-session, so the partial record can still carry the load up to the injury.

**When to apply** — Whenever the department logs injuries against GPS or session data. Eric's baseline: Catapult is the GPS stack, with a documented session lifecycle and data cleaning with spike detection (Explicit, Playbook p.7, pp.9-11). Inference: the cleaning step, or a missing export after an early stop, is the place where an injured session could be dropped; check that the partial session is retained and flagged. A practical first check: count how many non-contact injuries have a recorded session load for the day of injury.

**When NOT to apply** — This is the speaker's assertion about common practice in the literature, not a measured loss rate, and it comes from the NFL and European soccer. It does not by itself fix the confounding; the model adjustment is a separate step ([[framework--adjust-injury-models-for-same-session-load]]). Contact injuries are outside the speakers' definition, which is a non-contact injury that makes the player miss a subsequent session or match, in line with the UEFA definition (TIRINmtZOu0 [20:22], [20:53]); in the Q&A, the presenter who answers (after the question is handed to the other presenter at [19:52]; not identified by name in the captions) also says an off-field injury cannot be ruled out as training-related (TIRINmtZOu0 [20:22]).

**Example** — The speaker's own: a player injured in the middle of an NFL practice, where "the last thing they're worried about" is capturing the GPS data (TIRINmtZOu0 [17:49]).

# Keep the Load Record of the Session in Which an Injury Occurs

**What it is** — The speaker (Luke Bourne, caption spelling; named because the introduction lists "Luke Bourne and Patrick Ward" as presenters, Patrick hands over with "turn it over to Luke" at [10:10], and this passage refers back to "what Patrick was saying before" at [16:47]) says earlier studies did not use same-session load for a simple reason: when a player is injured mid-session, that session's data is "censored" or thrown out. His example is that nobody is going to "carefully extract the GPS unit" in the middle of the field during an NFL practice (TIRINmtZOu0 [17:18], [17:49]). The result is that the analysis sees load before the injury session but not the intensity of the session itself, which is the variable the speakers argue matters most (see [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]]). The speaker says analyses "need to account for" the session load in that session (TIRINmtZOu0 [17:49]) and names survival models (how intense it was until the moment of injury) as one route (TIRINmtZOu0 [18:19]). The speaker gives no figure for how much data is lost. Inference: an injured athlete's device often stops mid-session, so the partial record can still carry the load up to the injury.

**When to apply** — Whenever the department logs injuries against GPS or session data. Eric's baseline: Catapult is the GPS stack, with a documented session lifecycle and data cleaning with spike detection (Explicit, Playbook p.7, pp.9-11). # If a Coach Ignores the Report, Change the Question, Then Show Athletes Their Own Data

**What it is** — Three episodes from Morris's talk:
- **The trashed report.** He put a report he was "really proud of" on the offensive-line coach's desk and the coach threw it in the trash (QLdbKUiNadg [04:04]). His first reaction was that he had a PhD and was the expert; he then concluded that the coach told him "you're not having the right conversation," and he asks whether his data was; "in that case it wasn't" (QLdbKUiNadg [04:34]).
- **The reframe.** The coach said he wanted to see "how much they're bangin and practice" (caption) (QLdbKUiNadg [07:13]). Morris answered by first measuring the game (about 45 contacts, load per contact about 2.22) so the practice figures were comparable (QLdbKUiNadg [07:13], [07:45]).
- **Athlete buy-in.** Athletes must be "connected" to their data internally and externally, "because if you don't they don't have a lot of buy-in they feel like lab rats" (QLdbKUiNadg [17:38]). He mentions an earlier case, the Eagles under Chip Kelly, where, he says, players pushed back on being made to do more work (QLdbKUiNadg [17:38]).
He also notes that coaches grade in subjective terms, and without objective data a dispute is "just your opinion versus my opinion" (QLdbKUiNadg [01:02], [01:32]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's account is that the report answered a question the coach was not asking. He gives no evidence beyond his own experience. Inference: a coach's own question (here, contact in practice versus game) gets attention, while a generic report does not.

**When to apply** — When a coach does not read or use a report. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q6): "There is a place for the coach's eye: when something looks off, it can direct you where to look and gather data to investigate further." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q6)** Inference: the coach's question is the "where to look", and the data answer it. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q28): "Strength staff will build it most likely; we don't have sport science support for most teams." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q28)** Inference: at Baylor the person who reframes the report for the coach is often the strength staff member.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: anecdote, a single coach, a single athlete group. The talk does not report whether the reframed reports changed decisions or results. It does not support using data to win arguments with a coach; the speaker describes the reverse (first reaction: "you should listen to me", QLdbKUiNadg [04:34]). The Eagles reference is a second-hand recollection by the speaker.

# Strategic Naps: 15 to 20 Minutes, 30 Minutes or 90 Minutes, and Not When Night Sleep Is Poor

**What it is** — In the Q&A, the speaker (a sleep scientist, unnamed) says nine hours in bed means nine hours over a 24-hour period, so an athlete who cannot sleep it all at once can nap (J7smyg1Czik [29:33]). The speaker names three nap types: 15 to 20 minutes, after which you wake from light sleep and should feel refreshed; 30 minutes, which still ends in light sleep (stage two, the speaker says; the caption then garbles it as "a 13 minute nap"); and a 90-minute "granddaddy" nap that goes through light, deep and dream sleep, after which you wake spontaneously (J7smyg1Czik [29:33], [30:03]). The caution: if the athlete has trouble sleeping at night, a nap is "not a good thing," because "you're taking away from that sleep drive your homeostatic drive" (J7smyg1Czik [30:35]). The speaker also says trouble falling asleep in athletes usually comes from trying to sleep at an unusual time after crossing time zones (the example is four) or from heavy caffeine in the evening because games are in the evening (J7smyg1Czik [30:35]). The speaker adds that napping after training helps, since sleep consolidates learning and memory formed in training (J7smyg1Czik [25:25]).

# Baseball Analogies Break Where a Basketball Possession Can End With No Shot at All

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Seth part now") says many concepts port from baseball to basketball: rate stats over counting stats, efficiency, and treating the possession or shot like a plate appearance (BJkCqf6Fj2w [12:48], [13:18]). Past a certain level of detail, two differences matter (BJkCqf6Fj2w [13:18], [13:48], [14:18]):
- **No batting order.** In baseball "one through nine hits", but in basketball "there aren't turns"; a hot player can shoot every time down the court.
- **A third outcome.** A baseball plate appearance ends safe or out; a shot is made or missed, but "a very important third possibility" is "not shoot at all". "There's no equivalent of a pass in baseball."
Consequence the speaker draws: "a lot of what we would see as having a shot been contested well means that a player doesn't shoot at all" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [15:18]). He cites the corner three as the example: it is one of the most valuable shots yet a small share of attempts, "because you have to do something right beforehand" and the defense is trying to stop it (BJkCqf6Fj2w [14:48]).

**Why it works** — Stated by the speaker: because a possession has the option of not shooting, the defense's effect shows up in shots not taken, which a shot-level success rate cannot see (BJkCqf6Fj2w [14:18], [15:18]). The speaker gives no data for the corner-three share.

**When to apply** — When importing a metric or model from one sport to another. Inference: ask what the equivalent of "no shot" is in the new sport, an outcome the metric silently drops. At Baylor, the same question applies to any athlete-data measure where non-events (a test not taken, a session not logged) are missing, not zero. # Limits the Speaker Concedes: Forecast Gaps, Multi-Season Rebuilding and Single-Pick Scope

**What it is** — In Q&A four topics come up. Items 1 and 2 are limits Evan Monroe acknowledges; item 3 is a questioner's objection the speaker did not answer; item 4 is an extension he says is covered in the paper.
1. **Forecast quality.** Asked what happens if an early slump has another cause (a star missing half the season, then returning, or a trade), he says the policy relies on simulating the rest of the season well, as betting markets and draft simulators already do; known factors should go in. If something random happens and the team knows it and the league does not, "there could still be some opportunity to game" (-6pe_zOKCig [22:03], [22:33]). He suggests averaging forecasts from several sites or using an open forecasting tool (-6pe_zOKCig [22:33], [23:03]).
2. **Rebuilding.** A questioner worried that teams with no title hope might lose early and rebuild; he agrees this goes to the rebuilding strategy and the policy may increase that incentive (-6pe_zOKCig [13:58], [23:33]). One response: compute the optimal rule for past seasons, freeze the average, and quantify how much incentive that creates (-6pe_zOKCig [24:04]).
3. **Goal of the draft.** A questioner argued the draft's aim is to redistribute talent, not to reward the worst team, so a policy could produce more badly built teams; the questioner called it "a separate issue" and went on to ask about sensitivity, and the speaker did not respond to the goal point (-6pe_zOKCig [24:35], [25:06]).
4. **Multiple strong prospects.** The model extends to a sequential lottery by adding terms to the benefit from losing; an appendix in the paper covers it (-6pe_zOKCig [26:40], [27:10]).

**Why it works** — Not a mechanism claim; items 1 and 2 are the speaker's own acknowledgements, item 3 is a questioner's objection, and item 4 is an extension.

# In a Soccer Injury Model, Short- and Long-Term Workload and Detailed Injury History Mattered Most

**What it is** — The presenters report a gradient-boosted tree injury model (caption "XG boost") trained on injury-related features built from 2017-18 Premier League data and a historical career injury dataset (K5a7C4b1Cwc [03:02]). Inputs per player and match include workload from earlier selections, injury history (age, number of injuries) and context such as opponent and travel distance (K5a7C4b1Cwc [03:32], [04:03]). Using SHAP values, the least important group was contextual: travel to the game and rain. The next group, with somewhat more weight: days since the last injury, match-day temperature and age. The group that contributed most: the player's workload across matches, both short and long term, and the player's detailed injury history (K5a7C4b1Cwc [04:03], [04:33]). Testing: a 70/30 split with "five-block" cross-validation (caption spelling, probably five-fold), log loss 0.16, outperforming "many of the other base models we tested" (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:11], [09:42]); a Pearson correlation of 0.77 between the model's predictions and the 2018/19 Premier League season (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:42]). The talk does not say what was correlated (it reads as predicted versus observed injury outcomes) and gives no number of injuries or players.

**Why it works** — The speakers give no mechanism for why workload and injury history dominate; they report the SHAP ranking. Inference: prior injuries and recent load are the two inputs most directly tied to a specific player's tissue state, while travel and weather are shared across a squad.

**When to apply** — As a prior for what to log first when building an injury model with limited data: workload at more than one time scale, and a detailed injury history. Eric's baseline: there is no formal injury-risk model, and movement screens are collected and filed without changing programs (interview 2026-09-28, Q12, Explicit); this model's top inputs are workload and history, not screens.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the ranking is the model's own SHAP output, while the log loss and the 0.77 correlation validate predictions against a target the talk does not state ("with reality", K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:42]). Player load was imputed from event data by a separate model, because tracking data is not open (K5a7C4b1Cwc [17:53]); there was no club medical data and no training load, so the workload feature misses training exposure, which a questioner pressed (K5a7C4b1Cwc [18:24], [18:54]). One league, two seasons, soccer, professional players. The presenter says it is a decision framework, "not an expert medical prediction model" (K5a7C4b1Cwc [18:54]). A correlation of 0.77 and a log loss of 0.16 are reported without class balance, so how the model would rank athletes in practice is unknown. Existing library caution: ACWR-style workload features carry the confounding concern in [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]], which this model's authors do not address.

**Example** — The speakers' own: for a player facing Watford, the model takes his workload from the previous selections, his injury history and age, and the opponent and travel distance, and outputs an injury probability for that match (K5a7C4b1Cwc [03:32], [04:03]).

Injury risk: no formal model, ACWR distrusted, screens not acted on (Q12). Recovery and sleep: load design only, nothing objective tracked (Q23). Nutrition: no proactive data flow (Q24). Rehab and RTP: role stated (Q4, Q22) and a written protocol exists in the UE and LE templates (Q4a), not yet staged. Coaching stays thin: constraints-led coaching is not used (Q25), and the rest is unclaimed course material.

# Classify Chronotype, Then Time Peak Performance Relative to When the Athlete Wakes

**What it is** — A method the speaker (a sleep scientist by the speaker's own words, "sleep scientists like me", J7smyg1Czik [01:03]; unnamed) describes from a study the speaker attributes to a "university of Birmingham" (caption spelling) group. Competition-level athletes completed a paper-and-pencil morning-evening questionnaire, which classified them as early, intermediate or late (night owl) (J7smyg1Czik [17:22], [17:52]). Performance tests were done six times across the day: the bleep test (endurance, oxygen uptake) and sprint times, along with athletes' own ratings (J7smyg1Czik [17:52], [18:24]). As a whole group, performance was lowest at 7 am and highest in the late afternoon; the captions read "between four and seven" without am or pm (J7smyg1Czik [18:24], [18:55]). By chronotype, early types peaked between noon and 2, intermediate types in the mid-afternoon, and late types between 7 and 8 in the evening (J7smyg1Czik [18:55]). Relative to waking, early and intermediate types peaked about 6 to 7 hours after waking, and late types 11 hours or more after (J7smyg1Czik [19:58], [20:30]). A further analysis of a large number of athletes in 12 teams predicted team peak by team makeup: a team of mostly late types (T3) peaked later than a team of mostly early types (T10) (J7smyg1Czik [20:30], [21:00]). In the Q&A the speaker says the body clock shifts mostly with light and can be moved with light boxes and melatonin, for example, in the speaker's words, "when we send the Lions to London" the clock was shifted to earlier bedtimes, and that this takes discipline (J7smyg1Czik [29:02]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's account is that a biological clock decides whether someone is a night owl or morning lark, and everyone's peak therefore differs (J7smyg1Czik [16:51], [17:22]). The speaker's point is that a fixed wake time, imposed by a coach or schedule, does not shift when an individual peaks (J7smyg1Czik [19:58], [20:30]). The speaker gives no mechanism for the questionnaire's validity.

**When to apply** — When choosing the time of day for testing or high-stakes sessions, or when comparing an athlete's results across times. Inference: record each athlete's test time and, if the staff wishes, the questionnaire result, before comparing sessions; this matters for repeatable testing. Eric's baseline (course material, speaker unconfirmed, tagged Inferred): testing protocol has to be exactly repeatable over time ("how you do it in January needs to be the same as how you do it in April"). Eric's baseline: Eric has no stated chronotype practice; the baseline is silent.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the study is relayed second-hand from a "university of Birmingham" group (J7smyg1Czik [17:22]) with no citation and no n stated, and the 12-team result is a prediction ("they predicted performance", [20:30]), not an observed outcome. Sample sizes are not stated for the questionnaire study; the only count is 12 teams. The study is competition-level athletes, not college football, and early-morning football practice and meal schedules are not under athletes' control. The speaker says the whole circadian advantage is "unexplored" (J7smyg1Czik [23:03]). The claim that a third of the teams the speaker talks to are not interested is the speaker's own experience (J7smyg1Czik [28:31]). # Pricing a Protected Draft Pick as a Financial Option, in Basketball Units

**What it is** — Benjamin Foster (with co-author Michael Bins, caption spelling) prices a draft pick plus its protection scheme (a "draft pick asset") in player-value terms, not money (SIn6IyYQEVI [00:31], [01:02], [03:05]). A protection is a condition that lets the trading team keep the pick if it lands in a protected range, with the pick rolling over to later years (the Lakers 2015 pick was top-5 protected in 2015, top-3 for a couple of years, then unprotected in 2018) (SIn6IyYQEVI [02:02] to [03:05]). The analogy is a financial option: the protection plays the part of the contract terms, and the volatility of the underlying value matters (SIn6IyYQEVI [07:40], [08:10]). He does not use the option math directly, only its principles (SIn6IyYQEVI [08:10], [08:40]). Three steps (SIn6IyYQEVI [08:40]):
1. **Characterize volatility of the underlying asset.** Module one: an Elo-rating season simulation that gives a distribution of finishing position (1 means worst, to match how picks are dealt), run 10,000 times over the roughly 20 remaining games at the trade deadline (SIn6IyYQEVI [09:10], [09:40]). Module two: cumulative distributions of player value by pick position, using Basketball-Reference history for first-round picks, with win shares as the metric (SIn6IyYQEVI [10:11], [10:42]).
2. **Assess the contract conditions.** A 10,000-run Monte Carlo combines lottery probabilities and the protection scheme into a distribution of win shares summed over a player's first five years (SIn6IyYQEVI [11:14], [11:45]).
3. **Account for market risk** with a Wang transform (see [[heuristic--market-risk-preference-differs-by-pick-position-in-the-draft-pick-model]]), reducing the distribution to a single price (SIn6IyYQEVI [12:16], [13:17]).
He states the purpose is to help a team decide where to place protections when trading a pick away or trading for one (SIn6IyYQEVI [07:09]). Because millions of protection schemes exist, one base pick can have millions of trade values (SIn6IyYQEVI [04:07]). The model is modular, so the player value metric can be swapped (SIn6IyYQEVI [10:11], [19:23]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's reasoning is the option parallel: how likely the pick is to fall inside versus outside the protected range drives value (SIn6IyYQEVI [07:40]). He gives no tested argument that this transfer from finance is accurate; he says they adapt the principles "with our own methods" (SIn6IyYQEVI [08:40]).

**When to apply** — As a template for any asset that arrives as an uncertain outcome with contract conditions: model the uncertainty source, apply the conditions in simulation, then price. Inference: for Baylor, the closest analogs are recruiting and portal classes (an uncertain future player value) rather than any monitoring work; the applications note flags low direct use for Applied Performance. Eric's baseline: no direct link found.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: one worked example (see [[case-study--lakers-2015-pick-protections-removed-about-half-its-value]]), calibration from few pick-for-pick trades, and no outcome test. Limits the speaker names: the season simulation does not account for player movement, the work was done on personal computers with limited time, and time discounting and the option value of rolling a pick over are not explicitly modeled (SIn6IyYQEVI [14:48], [19:23], [22:26]). College rosters have no barter market with protections, so the option analogy may not carry over; the outcome data are NBA win shares for first-round picks only.

**Example** — The speaker's own: the Lakers 2015 first-round pick that went from the Suns to the Sixers at the 2015 deadline, priced with and without its top-5 protection (SIn6IyYQEVI [02:33], [12:46]).

# Pricing a Protected Draft Pick as a Financial Option, in Basketball Units

**What it is** — Benjamin Foster (with co-author Michael Bins, caption spelling) prices a draft pick plus its protection scheme (a "draft pick asset") in player-value terms, not money (SIn6IyYQEVI [00:31], [01:02], [03:05]). A protection is a condition that lets the trading team keep the pick if it lands in a protected range, with the pick rolling over to later years (the Lakers 2015 pick was top-5 protected in 2015, top-3 for a couple of years, then unprotected in 2018) (SIn6IyYQEVI [02:02] to [03:05]). The analogy is a financial option: the protection plays the part of the contract terms, and the volatility of the underlying value matters (SIn6IyYQEVI [07:40], [08:10]). He does not use the option math directly, only its principles (SIn6IyYQEVI [08:10], [08:40]). Three steps (SIn6IyYQEVI [08:40]):
1. **Characterize volatility of the underlying asset.** Module one: an Elo-rating season simulation that gives a distribution of finishing position (1 means worst, to match how picks are dealt), run 10,000 times over the roughly 20 remaining games at the trade deadline (SIn6IyYQEVI [09:10], [09:40]). Module two: cumulative distributions of player value by pick position, using Basketball-Reference history for first-round picks, with win shares as the metric (SIn6IyYQEVI [10:11], [10:42]).
2. **Assess the contract conditions.** A 10,000-run Monte Carlo combines lottery probabilities and the protection scheme into a distribution of win shares summed over a player's first five years (SIn6IyYQEVI [11:14], [11:45]).
3. **Account for market risk** with a Wang transform (see [[heuristic--market-risk-preference-differs-by-pick-position-in-the-draft-pick-model]]), reducing the distribution to a single price (SIn6IyYQEVI [12:16], [13:17]).
He states the purpose is to help a team decide where to place protections when trading a pick away or trading for one (SIn6IyYQEVI [07:09]). Because millions of protection schemes exist, one base pick can have millions of trade values (SIn6IyYQEVI [04:07]). The model is modular, so the player value metric can be swapped (SIn6IyYQEVI [10:11], [19:23]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's reasoning is the option parallel: how likely the pick is to fall inside versus outside the protected range drives value (SIn6IyYQEVI [07:40]). He gives no tested argument that this transfer from finance is accurate; he says they adapt the principles "with our own methods" (SIn6IyYQEVI [08:40]).

**When to apply** — As a template for any asset that arrives as an uncertain outcome with contract conditions: model the uncertainty source, apply the conditions in simulation, then price. Inference: for Baylor, the closest analogs are recruiting and portal classes (an uncertain future player value) rather than any monitoring work; the applications note flags low direct use for Applied Performance. Eric's baseline: no direct link found.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: one worked example (see [[case-study--lakers-2015-pick-protections-removed-about-half-its-value]]), calibration from few pick-for-pick trades, and no outcome test. Limits the speaker names: the season simulation does not account for player movement, the work was done on personal computers with limited time, and time discounting and the option value of rolling a pick over are not explicitly modeled (SIn6IyYQEVI [14:48], [19:23], [22:26]). College rosters have no barter market with protections, so the option analogy may not carry over; the outcome data are NBA win shares for first-round picks only.

**Example** — The speaker's own: the Lakers 2015 first-round pick that went from the Suns to the Sixers at the 2015 deadline, priced with and without its top-5 protection (SIn6IyYQEVI [02:33], [12:46]).

# Plan Rest Over a Rolling Horizon, Not Just the Next Match

**What it is** — Two points from the talk. First, the greedy rule of picking the best team for each match ignores long-term injury and absence risk, and the presenters found real coaches' selections closer to the greedy model (82% similar) than to their search model (76%), which they attribute to short-term job pressure (K5a7C4b1Cwc [10:12], [10:43], [14:48]). Second, in the Q&A, a questioner (not named) compared it to an American "survivor pool" in which picking the best matchups early corners you later, and suggested optimizing only the next X games and re-optimizing as injuries occur and player skill estimates change (K5a7C4b1Cwc [15:49], [16:20]). The presenter replied that the model has a parameter for how many games forward to simulate, from the end of the season to a five-game window moved forward week by week (K5a7C4b1Cwc [16:51]).

**Why it works** — The questioner's reason is that a short window lets the coach re-plan with real information on who is available (K5a7C4b1Cwc [16:20]); the presenter agrees the horizon can be set as a parameter (K5a7C4b1Cwc [16:51]). The presenter gives no result comparing a five-game window with a full-season horizon. Inference: a shorter horizon trades some foresight for robustness to model error, since injury and skill estimates drift.

**When to apply** — When planning rest or playing time across a congested stretch: set an explicit horizon (for example, the next several games), re-plan each week with updated availability, and name what the greedy option would be so the cost of the short-term choice is visible. Eric's baseline: in football the target is a peak every Saturday, with November and the postseason the priority window (interview 2026-09-28, Q14, Explicit), and bye weeks give players with few snaps harder practice (Q17, Explicit). Inference: those are horizon decisions already made by calendar, and the heuristic asks whether any are made match by match instead.

- claim--partial-ucl-tear-rest-study-43-players: "Clinical decisions belong to Athletic Medicine."

- claim--practice-contact-is-the-largest-exposure-lever-in-football: "A contact-practice decision is the coaching staff's with Athletic Medicine; Applied Performance supplies the count."
- framework--deepqb-receiver-target-model-inputs-and-four-variants: "NFL tracking data of a quality Baylor does not hold"

Exact edits (each old string occurs once in its file; verified with `grep -cF`):

1. `claim--hormone-measurement-methods-and-their-limits.md`
   - old: `(the speaker says she sees these "in my clinic all the time"; she does not say the patients are athletes)`
   - new: `(the speaker says these come up "in my clinic all the time"; the speaker does not say the patients are athletes)`
   - old: `Eric's baseline: "It's handled through training-load design alone.`
   - new: `Eric's baseline (on recovery and sleep): "It's handled through training-load design alone.`
2. `heuristic--strategic-nap-lengths-and-when-not-to-nap.md`
   - old: `The talk does not address timing relative to training or competition.`
   - new: `Beyond saying a nap after training helps (J7smyg1Czik [25:25]), the talk does not address how close to a session or competition a nap should end.`
3. `framework--classify-chronotype-and-time-peak-performance.md`
   - old: `The study is competition-level athletes, not college football, and early-morning football practice and meal schedules are not under athletes' control.`
   - new: `The study is competition-level athletes, not college football. The speaker notes that wake and training times are often set by the coach or by facility access, not by the athlete (J7smyg1Czik [19:58], [20:30], [23:55]).`
4. `heuristic--plan-rest-over-a-horizon-not-the-next-match.md`
   - old: `In football the roster and the game schedule give one game a week and no free rotation, so the "next X games" horizon is short already.`
   - new: `Inference: in football, with one game a week and little free rotation, the "next X games" horizon is short already.`
   - old: `the greedy-versus-search similarity numbers come from StatsBomb event data for two Premier League seasons, 2017/18 and 2018/19 (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:11], [10:12])`
   - new: `the data are StatsBomb event data from the 2017/18 and 2018/19 Premier League seasons, and the greedy comparison was run "for one season" (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:11], [09:42], [10:12])`
5. Bounded sweep: for each of the nine sentences listed above, either prefix it with "Inference:" or tie it to a `docs/method-baseline.md` line with that line's tag (the Athletic Medicine role lines may trace to Q4/Q22). Re-check the "no player salaries" sentence against current NCAA rules.

Optional nits, not counted: "Benjamin" to "Ben" (price-a-protected-draft-pick). Mark "Olin coach" as a caption spelling (show-coaches). In sleep-restriction, reconcile "durations not stated" with the speaker's "for a week".

After edits 1 to 5, promote. The sample found no systematic problem of the kinds the r4 reviewers flagged (untagged baseline lines, Q&A attribution to named people, smoothed number garbles). The remaining pattern is unlabelled Baylor-context reasoning in When NOT to apply, and the scan above bounds it.
